# Claude Code Parallel Worktrees — Boris Cherny's Canonical Workflow

**Category:** Claude Code workflow / productivity
**Confidence:** High — documented by Claude Code's creator on X/Threads, shipped as a native `--worktree` flag, and covered in official Anthropic docs.
**Primary sources:**
- Boris Cherny on X, "Do more in parallel": https://x.com/bcherny/status/2017742743125299476
- Boris Cherny on X, "Use claude --worktree for isolation": https://x.com/bcherny/status/2025007394967957720
- Anthropic official docs, "Orchestrate teams of Claude Code sessions": https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams
- "How Boris Uses Claude Code": https://howborisusesclaudecode.com/
- Community guides: shareuhack.com, thepromptshelf.dev, botmonster.com

---

## What it is

Boris Cherny — creator of Claude Code — runs **3 to 15 Claude Code sessions in parallel**, each in its own git worktree. It is, in his own words, "the single biggest productivity unlock" and "the top tip from the team." This pattern became the canonical Anthropic-internal workflow in late 2025 / early 2026 and got native CLI support via the `claude --worktree` flag.

The core insight is boring and load-bearing: **LLM coding is I/O-bound on the human, not the machine.** You spend 80% of your time reviewing, 20% typing the next prompt. If you run one Claude at a time, the model is idle while you read. If you run five, you are always reviewing *something* while the other four work. This is not "multi-agent orchestration" — it is single-operator parallelism. You are a director, not a coder.

Git worktrees are the enabling primitive because they give each session its own working directory on its own branch, sharing the same `.git` object store. Five worktrees = five isolated checkouts of the same repo, zero disk duplication of git history, zero merge conflicts between running sessions.

---

## How it works

### The git worktree primitive

`git worktree` is a vanilla git feature from 2015 that almost nobody uses. It lets one repo have multiple working directories:

```bash
# From inside a normal repo
git worktree add ../myproject-feature-a feature-a     # new branch
git worktree add ../myproject-bugfix main             # existing branch
git worktree list                                      # show all
git worktree remove ../myproject-feature-a            # clean up
```

Each worktree is a full checkout with its own `HEAD`, its own index, its own untracked files. They share the `.git` directory (via `.git` file pointing back to the main repo), so object storage is deduplicated. Branch safety is enforced: you can't check out the same branch in two worktrees simultaneously.

### The Boris pattern, step by step

1. **Start from a clean main.** `git checkout main && git pull`.
2. **Spin up N worktrees**, one per independent task:
   ```bash
   git worktree add ../proj-auth        -b feat/auth
   git worktree add ../proj-billing     -b feat/billing
   git worktree add ../proj-refactor    -b chore/refactor-api
   git worktree add ../proj-bugfix      -b fix/issue-412
   ```
3. **Open a terminal tab (or tmux pane) per worktree** and launch Claude in each:
   ```bash
   cd ../proj-auth     && claude
   cd ../proj-billing  && claude
   cd ../proj-refactor && claude
   cd ../proj-bugfix   && claude
   ```
4. **Prompt each session with one focused task.** One task = one worktree = one session. Do not multiplex tasks inside a single session.
5. **Cycle through the sessions while they work.** When one finishes, review, commit, push, open a PR, then either give it the next task or `git worktree remove` it.
6. **Merge back via normal PRs.** The worktrees never touch each other's filesystems; all coordination happens through git + PRs, the same as any human team.

### The `claude --worktree` shortcut

In late 2025 / early 2026 Anthropic shipped native worktree support so you do not have to manage them by hand:

```bash
claude --worktree                    # auto-creates a worktree, Claude picks the name
claude --worktree my-feature-name    # explicit name
claude --worktree --tmux             # also launch inside its own tmux session
```

This handles the `git worktree add`, `cd` into it, and launches Claude in one command. The Desktop app has had this for longer; it was ported to the CLI because the team realized everyone was doing it manually.

### Sub-agents with worktree isolation

The Task tool (sub-agents) can also be worktree-isolated. In your sub-agent frontmatter:

```yaml
---
name: migration-worker
isolation: worktree
---
```

When dispatched, the sub-agent gets its own worktree. When it finishes, the worktree path and branch name are returned to the parent agent for review/merge. This is the power move for large batched changes — migrations, codemod-style refactors, mass dependency bumps — where you want 10 sub-agents each handling a subdirectory without stomping on each other.

This is also the pattern behind Anthropic's "Agent Teams" feature (`code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams`): teammates coordinate through git commits in their respective worktrees.

---

## Quick start — 3-worktree minimum viable parallel workflow

```bash
# 1. From your project root on main
cd ~/projects/myproject
git checkout main && git pull

# 2. Create three worktrees beside the main checkout
git worktree add ../myproject-a -b task/a
git worktree add ../myproject-b -b task/b
git worktree add ../myproject-c -b task/c

# 3. Open three terminal tabs (or tmux windows) and launch Claude in each
# tab 1
cd ../myproject-a && claude
# tab 2
cd ../myproject-b && claude
# tab 3
cd ../myproject-c && claude

# 4. Prompt each with one focused task. Cycle between tabs.

# 5. When a task is done: review, commit, push, open PR
cd ../myproject-a
git add -A && git commit -m "feat: task a"
git push -u origin task/a
gh pr create --fill

# 6. Clean up after merge
git worktree remove ../myproject-a
```

Or, the native way:

```bash
claude --worktree task-a
claude --worktree task-b
claude --worktree task-c
```

Each command spawns a fresh Claude session in its own worktree in one line.

### With tmux (recommended for 5+ sessions)

Beyond ~4 terminal tabs, tmux becomes essential — you want a single keystroke to cycle through sessions and a persistent layout that survives terminal closure.

```bash
tmux new -s claude-parallel
# inside tmux
claude --worktree --tmux task-a    # spawns in its own tmux window
claude --worktree --tmux task-b
claude --worktree --tmux task-c
# Ctrl-b n / Ctrl-b p to cycle windows
```

Tools worth knowing:
- **`workmux`** (github.com/raine/workmux) — turns "create worktree + open tmux window + cd in + launch Claude" into one command.
- **`claude-tmux`** (github.com/nielsgroen/claude-tmux) — tmux popup TUI that manages multiple Claude Code sessions, worktrees, and PRs from one view.
- **`muxtree`** — simpler alternative with the same idea.

---

## When to use it (and when not to)

**Use parallel worktrees when:**
- You have **2+ genuinely independent tasks** — different files, different concerns, no shared state.
- You are doing a **large migration** where chunks can be parallelized (e.g. "convert all 40 React class components to function components").
- You are exploring **N alternative approaches** to the same problem and want to compare results side-by-side.
- You are **bug-hunting across multiple issues** and want each fix in its own branch/PR.
- You are **reviewing work on one task while another runs** — the "director mode" benefit.

**Do not use parallel worktrees when:**
- Tasks **depend on each other** — one needs the other's output. Chain them in a single session instead.
- You are **exploring an unfamiliar codebase** — you need focus, not five things shouting at you.
- You are **debugging a subtle issue** — context-switching kills debugging flow.
- You have **shared global state** outside git (a single dev database, a single running server on a single port). Two worktrees can't both `npm run dev` on port 3000.
- You are on a **laptop with <32GB RAM** and each session spawns heavy dev servers. Each worktree is a full checkout; if each runs webpack, you will OOM.

---

## What breaks at scale

Running 10–15 parallel sessions surfaces real problems:

1. **Port collisions.** Dev servers default to the same port. Fix: env vars per worktree (`PORT=3001`, `PORT=3002`), or a port-picker script.
2. **Database state.** SQLite is fine (each worktree gets its own file). Postgres/Mysql with a shared dev DB is a disaster — migrations from one worktree break another. Use per-worktree Docker containers, or schema namespaces.
3. **`node_modules` duplication.** Each worktree gets its own `node_modules`, which at 500MB–2GB × 10 = bad. Fix: pnpm with `shared-workspace-lockfile`, or a global store (`pnpm store`, `yarn berry pnp`).
4. **Review bottleneck shifts to you.** At ~5 sessions the model is no longer the bottleneck — *you* are. More parallelism past your review capacity is wasted.

title: Gemini CLI — Google's Free Terminal Coding Agent
guide_markdown:
# Gemini CLI — Google's Free Terminal Coding Agent

**GitHub:** https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli
**Stars:** ~101,000 (forks: ~13,000)
**License:** Apache 2.0
**Language:** TypeScript (Node.js)
**Repo path:** `repos/gemini-cli/` (clone pending — sandbox blocked git clone in this session; run `git clone https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli.git repos/gemini-cli` manually)

---

## What it is

Gemini CLI is Google's official open-source terminal-first AI coding agent. It's the direct Claude Code / Codex CLI competitor from Google, built on the Gemini 2.5 family of models. Unlike most "AI in the terminal" projects, it has a genuinely usable free tier: sign in with a personal Google account and you get **60 requests per minute and 1,000 requests per day** against Gemini 2.5 Pro at no cost. That alone makes it one of the highest-value free developer tools shipped in the last year.

It's an interactive REPL agent with tool use — it can read files, run shell commands, edit code, fetch URLs, search Google, and call MCP servers. Same basic loop as Claude Code: you type a request, it plans, it runs tools, it edits, you review, rinse, repeat.

Where Claude Code is polished and opinionated (tightly integrated with Anthropic's sandbox model), Gemini CLI is more raw and Google-flavored. It's a real, working agent — not a toy — but it leans on Google's strengths (huge context windows, cheap Flash tier, web grounding) rather than Anthropic's (tool discipline, long-horizon coherence).

## How it works

At runtime Gemini CLI is a Node.js TUI that:

1. Loads context from a `GEMINI.md` file in the current directory (same idea as `CLAUDE.md`)
2. Builds a system prompt with tool schemas for built-in tools (read, write, shell, glob, grep, web fetch, google search, memory)
3. Streams tokens from Gemini 2.5 Pro (default) or Flash (`-m gemini-2.5-flash`) via the chosen auth backend
4. Parses tool calls, prompts you for approval on destructive actions, runs them, feeds results back
5. Checkpoints conversations so you can resume

Built-in capabilities worth calling out:
- **Google Search grounding** — free live web search baked into the agent (Claude Code has to hit WebFetch/WebSearch separately)
- **MCP support** — add servers in `~/.gemini/settings.json`, same protocol as Claude Code, so your existing MCP catalog (Figma, GitHub, Playwright, Context7) works
- **`--include-directories`** — explicit multi-root context (`gemini --include-directories ../lib,../docs`)
- **Non-interactive mode** — `gemini -p "prompt" --output-format json` for scripting and CI, with `stream-json` for piping
- **GitHub Action** — official action for running Gemini CLI in CI

## System requirements

- Node.js 20+ (Node 22 LTS recommended)
- A Google account (free tier) OR a Gemini API key OR Vertex AI credentials
- Any OS with a terminal; works identically on macOS, Linux, WSL2, Windows
- Zero GPU/local model requirements — everything runs in Google's cloud

## Quick start

Install via npm (simplest on a dev machine that already has Node):

```bash
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
gemini
```

Or run with zero install:

```bash
npx @google/gemini-cli
```

macOS/Linux alternates:

```bash
brew install gemini-cli           # Homebrew
sudo port install gemini-cli      # MacPorts
```

On first run it prompts you to authenticate. Pick **"Sign in with Google"** for the 1K/day free tier — a browser tab opens, you sign in, token is stored in `~/.gemini/`. Done.

Switch models mid-session or at launch:

```bash
gemini -m gemini-2.5-flash        # much cheaper/faster, still strong
gemini -m gemini-2.5-pro          # default, best reasoning
```

Add MCP servers by editing `~/.gemini/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "playwright": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@playwright/mcp"] },
    "context7":   { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@upstash/context7-mcp"] }
  }
}
```

Drop a `GEMINI.md` in any repo to pin project context (coding standards, architecture notes, gotchas) — it's loaded automatically, same pattern as `CLAUDE.md`.

Non-interactive one-shot (great for scripts and hooks):

```bash
gemini -p "summarize the changes in the last 5 commits" --output-format json
```

## Gemini CLI vs Claude Code — honest comparison

| Dimension | Gemini CLI | Claude Code |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | **Free**: 60 req/min, 1K/day on personal Google | Paid: Pro/Max subscription or API credits |
| Model | Gemini 2.5 Pro / Flash | Claude Opus / Sonnet |
| Context window | ~1M tokens (Gemini 2.5 Pro) | ~200K tokens |
| Reasoning on hard multi-step code tasks | Good, sometimes loses the plot on long horizons | Best-in-class; more disciplined tool use |
| Tool approval UX | Functional, less polished | Tight, granular permissions |
| Web search | Built-in Google grounding (free) | WebSearch tool, requires API |
| MCP support | Yes | Yes |
| Sandboxing | Opt-in, less mature | Mature sandbox modes |
| Ecosystem (skills, plugins, hooks) | Smaller, growing | Large — AgentOps, superpowers, custom skills |
| Non-interactive / CI | Yes (`-p`, `--output-format json`, GitHub Action) | Yes (Claude Code SDK) |
| Offline | No | No |

**What Gemini CLI is better at:**
- Massive context tasks (read entire repos, summarize huge log files, refactor across dozens of files) — the 1M token window matters
- Free grunt work you don't want to burn Claude credits on (docs, boilerplate, commit messages, codegen from a spec)
- Scripted/batch automation where cost would add up
- Research tasks that need live web grounding without extra plumbing

**What Claude Code is better at:**
- Long multi-turn agentic work (the RPI/crank flywheel, subagent-driven dev, complex debugging)
- Tool-heavy workflows where tight permission control matters
- Anything where you've already invested in skills, hooks, and the AgentOps stack

## Known limitations

- Free tier is personal Google only — Workspace accounts often can't use it (admin policy blocks sign-in)
- 1K/day sounds like a lot but a single long agent session can chew through 100+ requests; heavy days hit the cap
- Tool discipline is weaker than Claude Code — it will sometimes run commands you didn't approve flow for, or stop and ask where Claude would have continued
- Less mature ecosystem: no native equivalent to the superpowers/AgentOps skill layer
- Model knowledge cutoff and training data bias differs — good Gemini answers on Google Cloud/Android/Flutter, relatively weaker on niche TS ecosystems where Claude shines

## How to use both together

The trick isn't "which one wins" — it's **routing**. Claude Code stays as the primary agent for high-value multi-step work (complex refactors, platform work, anything RPI-shaped). Gemini CLI becomes the free workhorse for:

1. **Commit/PR drudgery** — wire `gemini -p` into a git hook or the commit-commands skill to auto-draft commit bodies, PR descriptions, changelogs. Zero Claude credit burn.
2. **Large-context reads** — whenever a task needs to ingest an entire repo or huge log, hand it to Gemini first for a summary, then feed the summary to Claude. The 1M window is free leverage.
3. **Research + grounded web search** — `/research`-style tasks, documentation lookups, "what's the latest on X library" — Gemini's Google grounding is free and built-in.
4. **Codegen for throwaway scripts** — one-shot shell scripts, data munging, format converters. `gemini -p "write a bash script that..."` → done.
5. **CI jobs** — the official GitHub Action runs Gemini CLI on PRs for lint-style review, doc checks, test generation, without burning Anthropic quota.
6. **Second opinion / council member** — in `/council`-style multi-model workflows, Gemini is a free extra vote alongside Claude and Codex.
7. **Fallback during Anthropic rate limits or outages** — same terminal muscle memory, keeps you unblocked.

Practical setup: install it globally, sign in with Google, add the same MCP servers you use in Claude Code so context transfers cleanly, and keep a second terminal open for Gemini-handled tasks. Treat it like the free tier of a second brain.

## What we could build with it

- A **free commit/PR writer hook** that runs `gemini -p` on every commit and populates the body automatically
- A **large-repo summarizer** that indexes a codebase into `GEMINI.md` chunks so downstream Claude sessions start with perfect context
- A **research skill** that uses Gemini's grounded search for fact-gathering, then hands structured results to Claude for synthesis
- A **CI reviewer** using the official GitHub Action to do first-pass review on every PR for free before human/Claude review
- A **dual-agent council** where Claude and Gemini both critique a plan before implementation (poor-man's `/council`)
- A **terminal chatbot for docs/support** that only needs to answer questions and can run fully on the free tier

## Bottom line

Gemini CLI is the most valuable "free developer tool that's actually good" released recently. It doesn't replace Claude Code for re

title: Hunyuan3D-2 — Tencent's Open Image-to-3D Mesh Generator
guide_markdown:
# Hunyuan3D-2 — Tencent's Open Image-to-3D Mesh Generator

**GitHub:** https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hunyuan3D-2
**Latest:** Hunyuan3D-2.1 (PBR, production-ready materials) — https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hunyuan3D-2.1
**License:** Tencent Hunyuan Community License (open weights, some commercial restrictions for very large companies)
**Repo status:** Not cloned locally — the code is small (a few hundred MB) but model weights are 50 GB+ and are best pulled on demand from Hugging Face (`tencent/Hunyuan3D-2` and `tencent/Hunyuan3D-2.1`). Clone only when you're ready to run it.

---

## What it is

Hunyuan3D-2 is Tencent's open-source two-stage 3D asset generator. Feed it a single image and it returns a watertight 3D mesh with a textured (optionally PBR) surface, ready to drop into Blender, Unity, Unreal, or any standard DCC pipeline. It is the largest and most capable openly released image-to-3D model as of this writing, and it's the missing piece that has a companion: **HY-Motion** (Tencent's text-to-motion model), available at `~/projects/ai3-resources/repos/HY-Motion-1.0/`. Together they form a near-complete text → 3D character → animation pipeline (more on this below).

The release is actually a family of models, not a single checkpoint. There's a shape generator that hallucinates geometry from the image, a texture generator that paints the bare mesh, "Turbo" and "Fast" distilled variants for speed, a 600M "mini" variant for low-VRAM setups, and a multiview variant that takes 2–4 views of the same object for much better back/side reconstruction. Version 2.1 adds a full PBR texture stack (albedo / metallic-roughness / normal) so the outputs drop straight into a modern render engine without manual material fixup.

It is important to note: **Hunyuan3D-2 is image-to-3D only.** It does not natively read text prompts. The text-to-3D workflow everyone uses is "text → SDXL/Flux image → Hunyuan3D-2 mesh," which is what Tencent's own demos do internally. If you want single-call text-to-3D with open weights, this is not that tool — use Trellis or Tripo's hosted API for that (see `guides/blender-mcp-tripo-pipeline.md`).

---

## How it works under the hood

**Stage 1 — Shape generation (Hunyuan3D-DiT).** A diffusion transformer operating in a latent 3D representation. The input image is encoded by a DINOv2-style vision encoder; the DiT denoises a latent volume conditioned on those features; a VAE decoder reconstructs an SDF (signed distance field) which is marched to a triangle mesh. The model was trained on tens of millions of 3D assets with rendered multiview supervision.

- `Hunyuan3D-DiT-v2-0` — 1.1B params, standard quality
- `Hunyuan3D-DiT-v2-0-Fast` — 1.1B, guidance-distilled (fewer CFG steps)
- `Hunyuan3D-DiT-v2-0-Turbo` — 1.1B, step-distilled (6–8 steps vs 50)
- `Hunyuan3D-DiT-v2-mini` — 0.6B, low-VRAM variant
- `Hunyuan3D-DiT-v2-mv` — 1.1B multiview — feed 2–4 images of the same object
- `Hunyuan3D-DiT-v2-1` — 3.0B, v2.1 release with new VAE and PBR-aware geometry

**Stage 2 — Texture generation (Hunyuan3D-Paint).** A multi-view diffusion model that paints the bare mesh. It renders the mesh from 6+ canonical viewpoints, diffuses textures on each view jointly (with cross-view attention for consistency), then bakes them back into a UV atlas. v2.1's Paint model outputs a full PBR set.

- `Hunyuan3D-Paint-v2-0` — 1.3B standard
- `Hunyuan3D-Paint-v2-0-Turbo` — 1.3B distilled
- v2.1 Paint — adds albedo / metallic-roughness / normal outputs

Output is always a `trimesh.Trimesh` object, which you can export as **GLB, OBJ, PLY, STL, FBX** — anything trimesh supports. GLB is the recommended default since it embeds textures and PBR materials in one file.

---

## System requirements

Be honest with yourself about VRAM. This is a big model.

**Hunyuan3D-2.0:**
- Shape only: **6 GB VRAM** (mini) to ~10 GB (DiT-v2-0)
- Shape + texture: **16 GB VRAM** total
- Fits on a single 3090, 4080, or 4090 comfortably. A 12 GB 3060 can run shape-only or the mini variant.

**Hunyuan3D-2.1 (PBR):**
- Shape only: **10 GB VRAM**
- Texture only: **21 GB VRAM**
- Shape + texture together: **29 GB VRAM**
- You want a **4090, A6000, or better** for the full 2.1 pipeline. A single 24 GB card can do 2.1 shape + 2.0 texture as a hybrid.

**Disk:** model weights are ~50 GB across shape + texture for v2.1. Keep them on an NVMe — loading is I/O bound.

**Software:** Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.1+ with CUDA 11.8 or 12.1, a C++ toolchain for the custom rasterizer/renderer. Linux is the happy path; Windows works via WSL2 or YanWenKun's WinPortable build (https://github.com/YanWenKun/Hunyuan3D-2-WinPortable). macOS works for shape only via MPS — texture gen is effectively CPU-bound and unbearably slow. There's also a GPU-poor fork at https://github.com/deepbeepmeep/Hunyuan3D-2GP that offloads aggressively for 8 GB cards.

---

## Quick start

```bash
# clone code (small)
cd ~/projects/ai-catalogs/repos/
git clone https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hunyuan3D-2.git
cd Hunyuan3D-2

# python env
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.3.0 torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .

# build the custom rasterizer + renderer (required for texture gen)
cd hy3dgen/texgen/custom_rasterizer && python setup.py install && cd ../../..
cd hy3dgen/texgen/differentiable_renderer && python setup.py install && cd ../../..

# weights auto-download from HF on first run; or preload:
huggingface-cli download tencent/Hunyuan3D-2 --local-dir ./weights
```

Minimal image-to-mesh script:

```python
from hy3dgen.shapegen import Hunyuan3DDiTFlowMatchingPipeline
from hy3dgen.texgen import Hunyuan3DPaintPipeline
from PIL import Image

img = Image.open("reference.png")

shape_pipe = Hunyuan3DDiTFlowMatchingPipeline.from_pretrained("tencent/Hunyuan3D-2")
mesh = shape_pipe(image=img)[0]          # trimesh.Trimesh
mesh.export("bare.glb")

paint_pipe = Hunyuan3DPaintPipeline.from_pretrained("tencent/Hunyuan3D-2")
textured = paint_pipe(mesh, image=img)
textured.export("final.glb")
```

For the Turbo variants, swap the pretrained name to `tencent/Hunyuan3D-2/hunyuan3d-dit-v2-0-turbo` and drop inference steps to 6. For v2.1 with PBR, use `tencent/Hunyuan3D-2.1`.

There is also a Gradio app (`python app.py`), an API server (`python api_server.py`), and a ComfyUI integration documented at https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/3d/hunyuan3D-2 — ComfyUI is the path of least resistance if you already use it for SDXL/Flux work.

---

## How image-to-mesh differs from text-to-mesh

Text-to-3D tools (Shap-E, Point-E, early DreamFusion) hallucinate geometry from a text prompt alone. They're fast but vague — "a red sports car" gives you something car-shaped but generic and blurry. Image-to-3D is the dominant paradigm now because it cleanly separates concerns: let a mature 2D generator (SDXL, Flux, Midjourney) handle creative ideation and composition, then let a specialist 3D model do what it's good at — recovering geometry from pixels it can see.

Concretely with Hunyuan3D-2:
- **Better silhouette lock.** The reference image pins the silhouette exactly, so the mesh matches what you designed.
- **Style transfers cleanly.** The texture stage paints the mesh using the reference image as conditioning, so a stylized anime ref produces a stylized mesh, not a photoreal one.
- **Front-bias problem.** Single-view input means the back of the object is a hallucination. Use the **mv (multiview)** variant with 2–4 orthogonal views if you care about the back — it's the single biggest quality unlock.
- **Workflow cost.** You pay a 2D generation step upfront. Worth it. A Flux image → Hunyuan3D-2 mesh takes ~30 s on a 4090 and beats any pure text-to-3D open model.

---

## Integration with HY-Motion — the full pipeline

If you have HY-Motion cloned at `~/projects/ai3-resources/repos/HY-Motion-1.0/`. HY-Motion generates SMPL-X skeletal motion from text ("a character doing a backflip"). Hunyuan3D-2 generates a static character mesh from an image. Chained, you get:

1. **Text prompt** → Flux/SDXL → character reference image
2. **Character image** → Hunyuan3D-2 (mv variant for quality) → textured GLB
3. **Auto-rig** → Mixamo auto-rigger, Blender's Rigify, or Meshy's auto-rig endpoint
4. **Motion prompt** → HY-Motion → SMPL-X animation
5. **Retarget** → Blender (use the Rokoko or Auto-Rig Pro retargeter) → final animated character
6. **Render** → Blender Eevee/Cycles, or export FBX to Unity/Unreal

The weak link in this chain is step 3 (auto-rigging). Hunyuan3D-2 doesn't output rigs. Mixamo works for humanoid bipeds, breaks on anything else. For non-humanoid creatures you'll need manual rigging or a tool like AnythingWorld.

This is a genuinely powerful pipeline for indie game devs, VTuber creators, and previs artists. No existing commercial product bundles it this way.

---

title: llms.txt — The Website Manifest for LLM Agents
guide_markdown:
# llms.txt — The Website Manifest for LLM Agents

**Spec site:** https://llmstxt.org
**Proposal (Sep 2024):** Jeremy Howard, Answer.AI — https://www.answer.ai/posts/2024-09-03-llmstxt.html
**Reference repo:** https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt
**Adoption (Oct 2025, BuiltWith):** ~844,000 sites
**Canonical location:** `/llms.txt` at the domain root (alongside `robots.txt`)

> **One-line framing.** `llms.txt` is the file you put at the root of your website so that LLM agents — Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Cursor, Gemini, whatever — can figure out what your site *is* and *what matters on it* without having to crawl, render, and guess from the HTML. It's the "manifest" layer for AI-era web discovery, sitting next to `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` but aimed at a different reader.

---

## What it is

`llms.txt` is a proposed standard, introduced by Jeremy Howard (fast.ai / Answer.AI) in September 2024, for a single Markdown file hosted at the root of a website that gives large language models a compact, structured, high-signal overview of the site. The format is unusual in one important way: it uses **Markdown**, not XML or JSON, specifically because the consumer is a language model that already parses Markdown natively and benefits from prose context around link lists.

There are two companion artifacts:

1. **`/llms.txt`** — the short, curated index. Think of it as "here is what this site is, and here are pointers to the dozen or so pages that actually matter." This file is meant to fit comfortably in a model's context window.
2. **`/llms-full.txt`** — an optional, much longer file (co-developed by Mintlify and Anthropic) that inlines the *full Markdown* of every important page in one document. Useful when you want an agent to have the entire docs corpus in a single fetch without walking links.

Both live at predictable, fixed paths at the domain root. There is no registration, no API, no keys. It is a web standard in the Robots Exclusion Protocol tradition: just drop a file, and the agents that care will find it.

### How it differs from existing web metadata files

| File | Primary reader | Purpose | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| `robots.txt` | Crawlers | Tell bots where they may and may not go | Line-based directives |
| `sitemap.xml` | Search engines | List every URL for exhaustive indexing | XML |
| `humans.txt` | Humans | Credit the team behind a site | Free-form text |
| **`llms.txt`** | **LLM agents** | **Explain what the site is and which pages carry the meaning** | **Markdown** |
| `llms-full.txt` | LLM agents | Inline full content of key pages in one doc | Markdown |

The critical distinction is *curation vs. exhaustiveness*. A sitemap is a phonebook: every URL, flat, no commentary. `llms.txt` is an index card on the front of the site that says "here is what we do, and here are the ten links an agent should read first." Search engines can afford to crawl 50,000 URLs; an LLM agent answering a user question has a 200k-token budget and 3 seconds. The whole point is to make the agent's first fetch the one that actually matters.

`robots.txt` governs *access*. `llms.txt` governs *attention*. They are complementary, not competing.

---

## How it works

### The spec, condensed

The format is deliberately minimal. The only hard requirement is a single H1 at the top. Everything else is recommended but optional.

```markdown
# Project or Site Name

> Optional one-paragraph description as a Markdown blockquote. This is the
> "elevator pitch" the model will read first. Keep it tight — one or two
> sentences that a model can use as a summary when someone asks "what is
> this site?"

Optional free-form Markdown prose giving extra context: who runs the site,
what it's for, any important caveats, how the content is organized. You
can link freely; links here are treated as inline references.

## Docs

- [Getting Started](https://example.com/docs/getting-started): One-line description of what this page covers.
- [API Reference](https://example.com/docs/api): The full REST API.
- [CLI Guide](https://example.com/docs/cli): Command-line usage.

## Examples

- [Tutorial: Hello World](https://example.com/examples/hello): Minimal walkthrough.
- [Cookbook](https://example.com/examples/cookbook): Common recipes.

## Optional

- [Changelog](https://example.com/changelog): Release history.
- [Blog](https://example.com/blog): Long-form writing.
```

**Rules of the road:**

- **H1 is required.** It's the name of the site/project. Exactly one.
- **Blockquote is the summary.** If present, it goes immediately after the H1, and it's the single most important piece of metadata.
- **H2 sections group links.** Common section names in the wild: `Docs`, `Examples`, `API`, `Guides`, `Blog`, `Policies`, `Optional`.
- **Each link is a bullet of the form `[Title](URL): one-line description`.** The description is what the model uses to decide whether to fetch the link.
- **An `## Optional` section is treated as lower priority.** Models that are context-constrained may skip it entirely. Use it for "nice to have but not load-bearing" links.
- **All URLs should be absolute** (full `https://...`), not relative, because agents may fetch this file from cache or a mirror.

That's the whole spec. No versioning headers, no front-matter, no required metadata fields. Plain Markdown a human can hand-write in five minutes.

### The `llms-full.txt` variant

`llms-full.txt` takes every page in your "Docs" section (or whatever you consider canonical) and concatenates the raw Markdown of each page into one file, with `## Page Title` headers separating them. The goal is "single fetch, full context." This was co-developed by Mintlify and Anthropic and is now part of the broader proposal. Anthropic, Stripe, Vercel, Cursor, Cloudflare, Pinecone, and Windsurf all publish one.

Rule of thumb:
- **`llms.txt`** → index of pointers, always ship this.
- **`llms-full.txt`** → inlined body, ship this if your docs are < ~500k tokens and you want agents to have one-shot access.

### Companion: `.md` versions of every page

The third leg of the proposal is that every HTML page should also be served as a plain Markdown version at the same URL with a `.md` suffix (e.g., `example.com/docs/api` → `example.com/docs/api.md`). This is what `nbdev`, Mintlify, Fern, and a growing number of docs platforms now do automatically. It lets an agent fetch a clean, parser-friendly version of any page linked from `llms.txt` without having to scrape HTML. Fern goes a step further and detects LLM bot user-agents and serves the Markdown version directly at the original URL, claiming a 90%+ token reduction versus rendered HTML.

---

## Key mechanics

### Who's adopted it

As of late 2025, real `llms.txt` files in production include:

- **Anthropic** (docs.anthropic.com/llms.txt) — the flagship reference implementation, co-developed with Mintlify.
- **Stripe**, **Cloudflare**, **Vercel**, **Supabase** — canonical dev-tool adopters.
- **Cursor**, **Windsurf** — AI-native IDEs that both publish and consume.
- **Pinecone**, **Coinbase**, **Mintlify**, **Perplexity** — AI infra and docs-heavy companies.
- Every site hosted by **Mintlify**, **Fern**, **Docusaurus (via plugin)**, **GitBook**, and several other docs platforms — these auto-generate `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` on build, which is how adoption jumped from "a handful of early movers" to ~844k sites in under 12 months.

Notable *non*-adopters: most CMS-based marketing sites, most WordPress blogs, and most e-commerce storefronts. The long tail is still wide open.

### Who reads it

Consumption is less well-documented than publication, but in practice:

- **Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, Continue, Aider** — when pointed at a library, many will check `/llms.txt` before crawling the docs site.
- **Perplexity and ChatGPT's browsing/search modes** — will opportunistically read `llms.txt` when building a retrieval plan.
- **Agent frameworks** (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Mastra, CrewAI) — have helpers/loaders for fetching `llms-full.txt` as a one-shot document source.
- **Claude's WebFetch tool** — does not yet auto-prefer `llms.txt`, but will honor it if you instruct the agent to check.

The honest state of the world: publication is ahead of consumption. Shipping `llms.txt` today is primarily a bet on the near-future agent web, plus a free SEO/GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) signal that costs 30 minutes to put in place.

### Tools that generate it

- **Mintlify** — auto-generates `/llms.txt`, `/llms-full.txt`, and `.md` versions of every page for all hosted docs. Zero config.
- **Fern** — same, plus the bot-detection serve-Markdown-at-original-URL trick.
- **`llmstxt` npm / Python packages** — scrape a sitemap and produce a draft `llms.txt` you can hand-edit.
- **llmstxtgenerator.org, seomator.com, Mintlify's free generator** — web-based form-fill tools for non-technical site owners.

# n8n-mcp + obsidian-skills — Two High-Leverage Claude Code Extensions

Two of the most useful community-built extensions to Claude Code as of April 2026. Both are in the same category — *"expose a large, structured external system to Claude so it can reason about it natively"* — but they attack very different domains: **n8n-mcp** (czlonkowski) unlocks workflow automation, and **obsidian-skills** (kepano) unlocks personal knowledge management. Covered in one guide because they're architectural siblings and often end up installed together on the same workbench.

---

## Part 1: n8n-mcp — 1,396 n8n nodes exposed to Claude

**Author:** Romuald Czlonkowski (@czlonkowski)
**Repo:** https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp
**License:** MIT
**Stars:** ~17.8k (as of April 2026) — one of the most successful community MCP servers.

### What it is

An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that loads every n8n node's schema, documentation, and operation metadata into a searchable database and exposes it to Claude as tools. With it installed, Claude can *natively* design, validate, and (optionally) deploy n8n workflows without hallucinating node names, property shapes, or connection rules.

n8n is a workflow automation platform (think Zapier, but self-hostable and massively more powerful). It has ~1,400 nodes covering every major SaaS, database, LLM, file format, and protocol. The problem: that's too much surface area for an LLM to know from training alone — Claude will cheerfully invent nodes that don't exist, miss required fields, and wire up connections that won't run. n8n-mcp fixes that by making node metadata a first-class tool Claude can query.

### How it works under the hood

- **Database:** better-sqlite3 (default, native) or sql.js fallback. Pre-built, ships with the package.
- **Coverage (as of latest release):**
  - 1,396 nodes total (812 core + 584 community)
  - 99% property coverage with detailed schemas
  - 63.6% operation coverage
  - 87% documentation coverage pulled from the official n8n docs
  - 265 AI-capable tool variants fully documented
  - 2,646 pre-extracted configurations from popular templates
  - 2,709 complete workflow templates with metadata
- **Two modes:**
  1. **Documentation-only mode** — no n8n instance required. Claude can search nodes, read schemas, validate workflow JSON, and generate workflow files. You copy-paste the output into n8n yourself.
  2. **Full mode** — give it `N8N_API_URL` + `N8N_API_KEY` and Claude can create, update, execute, and monitor workflows directly in your n8n instance.
- **Tools exposed to Claude** (selected):
  - Search nodes by name, category, or capability
  - Fetch a node's full property schema
  - Validate a workflow JSON before execution
  - Browse templates by use case
  - Filter community nodes by verified status
  - (Full mode) create/update/execute workflows, read execution logs

### Key mechanics

**Installation (5 options, ranked by likely preference):**

1. **NPX (quickest local)** — no install, just point Claude at the binary:
   ```bash
   npx n8n-mcp
   ```
2. **Docker** — pre-built image:
   ```bash
   docker pull ghcr.io/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp:latest   # ~280MB
   ```
3. **Hosted free tier** at dashboard.n8n-mcp.com — 100 tool calls/day, API key signup only. Zero install.
4. **Railway one-click** — if you want a persistent cloud MCP.
5. **Local dev clone** — for hacking on it. Clone, `npm install`, `npm run build`, point Claude at `dist/index.js`.

**Claude Code configuration (documentation-only, safest default):**

Add to `~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` (Linux) or `~/.claude/settings.json` for Claude Code:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "n8n-mcp": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["n8n-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "MCP_MODE": "stdio",
        "LOG_LEVEL": "error",
        "DISABLE_CONSOLE_OUTPUT": "true"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**The `MCP_MODE: "stdio"` env var is required** — without it, the server writes log noise to stdout and Claude Code fails to parse the JSON-RPC stream. This is gotcha #1.

**Full mode (Claude can deploy workflows directly):**

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "n8n-mcp": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["n8n-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "MCP_MODE": "stdio",
        "LOG_LEVEL": "error",
        "DISABLE_CONSOLE_OUTPUT": "true",
        "N8N_API_URL": "http://localhost:5678",
        "N8N_API_KEY": "your-n8n-api-key-here",
        "WEBHOOK_SECURITY_MODE": "moderate"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

For Docker, swap the n8n URL to `http://host.docker.internal:5678`.

**Privacy:** Telemetry is on by default. Disable with `N8N_MCP_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true`.

### Quick start

```bash
# 1. Install the MCP in Claude Code config (see above)
# 2. Restart Claude Code so it picks up the new MCP server
# 3. In any conversation, just ask:

> Build me an n8n workflow that watches a Gmail inbox for invoices,
  extracts the PDF attachment, runs it through the OpenAI node to pull
  out vendor/amount/date, appends to a Google Sheet, and posts a
  summary to Slack.

# Claude will:
#  - query n8n-mcp for the Gmail, PDF Extract, OpenAI, Sheets, Slack nodes
#  - read their actual schemas (not hallucinate)
#  - validate the workflow JSON against the MCP's validator
#  - return a complete workflow.json you can import into n8n
#  - (full mode) deploy it directly to your n8n instance
```

### Gotchas

1. **Never point full-mode MCP at your production n8n.** The docs are emphatic: always work on a dev instance. The MCP has no undo and Claude can edit any workflow it can see.
2. **`MCP_MODE: "stdio"` is mandatory** for Claude Code. Omit it and you get opaque JSON parsing errors.
3. **Memory footprint:** better-sqlite3 uses ~100-120MB; sql.js fallback ~150-200MB. Fine on a dev machine, worth knowing on a resource-constrained server.
4. **Webhook security:** Default "strict" blocks localhost webhooks. For local dev, set `WEBHOOK_SECURITY_MODE=moderate`.
5. **Coverage isn't 100%.** Operation coverage is 63.6% — rarer nodes may have incomplete action metadata. Claude will tell you when it's extrapolating vs. reading from the DB.

### What we could build with it

- **Automated n8n workflow generator from natural language** — the obvious one, and the headline feature.
- **Workflow audit / simplification pipeline** — feed a messy existing n8n export to Claude, let it use the MCP to rewrite it cleaner.
- **n8n + trading integration** — for you's trading agent team, n8n could orchestrate off-chain triggers (news sentiment, social signals, funding rate webhooks) feeding into the Legion Command decision layer. n8n-mcp lets Claude design those pipelines fluently.
- **Self-editing workflows** — pair n8n-mcp with a scheduled Claude job (via the `schedule` skill) that reviews the previous day's executions and proposes workflow improvements.
- **Template gallery search** — with 2,709 templates in the MCP database, Claude becomes a natural-language template browser.

---

## Part 2: obsidian-skills — Kepano's Obsidian toolkit for Claude

**Author:** Stephan Ango (@kepano) — CEO of Obsidian, well-known in the PKM/note-taking community.
**Repo:** https://github.com/kepano/obsidian-skills
**License:** Check repo
**Status:** Active, following the emerging "Agent Skills" specification.

### What it is

A collection of **five agent skills** built to the open Agent Skills specification, designed to let any skills-compatible agent (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, etc.) work directly with Obsidian vaults. The skills handle Obsidian's specific flavors of markdown, its Bases feature (database views over notes), JSON Canvas files, and vault CLI operations.

The point: Obsidian is the dominant markdown PKM system. Claude Code is the dominant coding agent. Until obsidian-skills, there was no clean way for Claude to read, write, or manipulate an Obsidian vault while respecting Obsidian's conventions (wikilinks, properties, callouts, templates, Bases formulas). Kepano — literally the CEO of Obsidian — shipped the reference implementation.

### The five skills

1. **`obsidian-markdown`** — Create and edit **Obsidian Flavored Markdown**. Handles:
   - Wikilinks (`[[Note Name]]`, `[[Note Name|alias]]`)
   - Embeds (`![[Note Name]]`, `![[image.png]]`)
   - Callouts (`> [!note]`, `> [!warning]`)
   - Properties (YAML frontmatter with Obsidian-specific types: `tags`, `aliases`, date types)
   - Block references (`[[Note Name#^block-id]]`)
2. **`obsidian-bases`** — Create and manipulate **Obsidian Bases** (the database-view-over-notes feature introduced in 2025). Handles views, filters, formulas, summaries. This is the only tool outside Obsidian itself that understands Bases syntax.
3. **`json-canvas`** — Work with **JSON Canvas** files (the open spec Obsidian uses for its infinite canvas feature). Create nodes, edges, groups, connections — perfect for agent-generated mind maps or visual plans.
4. **`obsidian-cli`** — Shell-level interaction with Obsidian vaults. Useful for plugin deve
